Lesson framework

Investigation · p. 90

Three Relationships in Communities

Examine each pairing. Who is benefiting? Is the other organism helped, harmed, or unaffected?
07 / 41
Investigation pair 1 of 3

Cattle Egrets & Cattle

Cattle kick up insects and worms while grazing — and egrets eat them. The egret benefits (+); the cattle are unaffected (0).
08 / 41
Investigation pair 2 of 3

Bees & Beebalm Flowers

Bees collect nectar to make honey. As they travel between flowers, they transfer pollen — which the flowers need to make seeds. Both benefit (+/+).
09 / 41
Investigation pair 3 of 3

Fleas, Ticks & Pets

Fleas and ticks live on a host, feeding on blood. The parasite benefits (+); the host is harmed (−) and can get sick. Three pairings, three different patterns.
10 / 41
Vocabulary · p. 91

What is Symbiosis?

SYMBIOSIS is a close, long-term relationship between two species that usually involves an exchange of food or energy. The two organisms live in direct contact.
11 / 41
The textbook's anchor example

Barbel Fish & Hippopotamuses

Barbel fish follow and groom hippos. The fish gets food (parasites + dead skin); the hippo gets cleaned. Both rely on this interaction to stay healthy and survive. This is the model for symbiosis.
12 / 41
Where symbiosis lives

Coral Reefs — A Symbiosis Hotspot

Communities around the world include symbiotic relationships, but coral reefs are especially rich in them — clownfish, sea anemones, cleaner wrasses, even microscopic copepods all live in symbiosis.
13 / 41
Collect Evidence A · p. 88

Back to the Shrimp & Eel

The cleaner shrimp and moray eel have the same pattern as the barbel fish and hippo. Record this as Evidence A on p. 88 — Lesson 2 will give you more types of symbiosis to compare.

Three Types of Symbiosis

Who Benefits? Who Gets Harmed?

Every symbiotic relationship can be sorted by a simple + / 0 / − outcome for each species.
18 / 41
Symbiosis Type 1 of 3

Commensalism — Epiphytes on Trees

Epiphytes (EH-puh-fites) — like orchids and bromeliads — grow on tree trunks. They get living space and sunlight. The tree is neither helped nor harmed. + / 0
19 / 41
Symbiosis Type 2 of 3

Parasitism — One Wins, One Loses

A parasite benefits; the host is harmed. The two species are in direct contact, often for the parasite's whole life. + / −
20 / 41
Symbiosis Type 3 of 3

Mutualism — Clownfish & Anemone

The clownfish gets protection (anemones sting its predators). The anemone gets energy from clownfish waste. Both win. + / +
21 / 41
A Closer Look · p. 96

The African Oxpecker

Two species of African oxpecker perch on large mammals — impalas, water buffalo, zebras, rhinos, giraffes — and feed on ticks and insects living on them. Sounds like a clear case of mutualism… but is it?
22 / 41
Scientists are still investigating

Friend or Foe?

As scientists collected new evidence, the oxpecker story got more complicated. This is what science actually looks like — we revise our thinking as new data comes in.
23 / 41
Not all relationships are symbiotic

Three More Relationship Types

Not all community interactions involve direct, long-term contact. Three more relationships matter: cooperative, predator-prey, and competitive.
24 / 41
Non-symbiotic type 1 of 3

Cooperative — Leafcutter Ants

Organisms in the same population work together for survival. Leafcutter ants carry leaves to grow fungus for food. Elephants raise young together. Squirrel monkeys hunt as a group.
25 / 41
Non-symbiotic type 2 of 3

Predator-Prey — Osprey & Fish

One organism (the predator) eats another (the prey). The osprey catches a fish. + / − — predator benefits, prey is harmed.
26 / 41
Why predators matter

Predators Keep Prey Healthy

Predators often capture weak or injured prey. Removing them leaves more resources for the rest of the prey population — keeping it healthy and within the ecosystem's carrying capacity.
27 / 41
Non-symbiotic type 3 of 3

Competitive — Wolves & Ravens

Two or more organisms need the same resource at the same time. Wolves and ravens compete for meat. Tall trees compete with younger trees for sunlight. − / − — both lose something.
28 / 41
Lesson 2 wrap

Six Relationship Types

Three symbiotic, three non-symbiotic. Each has a unique pattern of who benefits and who doesn't.
